headline: High risk of prompt injection and cascading errors: ctx can observe Claude Code events while OpenHands runs shell/browser/MCP actions in a writable runtime.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code PostToolUse and Stop events, so it can ingest agent-generated content; OpenHands can use MCP and browser/shell actions, creating a plausible instruction-injection path if its outputs are fed into ctx. The shared bridge is not fully documented, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF OpenHands outputs are forwarded into ctx without provenance filtering, injection is possible.
IF ctx treats observed tool output as trusted instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer behavior.
mitigations: Add provenance tags to all OpenHands outputs before ctx ingests them.
Disable automatic instruction parsing on observed tool output.
Require a human review step for any tool output that contains imperative language.
requires-engineering: isolate the two agents onto separate channels with explicit allowlists.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers, while OpenHands reads and writes files in a runtime sandbox and handles model-provider API keys. If they share mounted files or logs, sensitive runtime data can flow between them; the profiles show a plausible shared-file path but not a guaranteed one.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same workspace or log volume, data can leak between them.
IF OpenHands writes secrets or file contents into shared files, ctx can read them.
mitigations: Use separate volumes for ctx and OpenHands.
Rotate and scope any model-provider API keys used by OpenHands.
Block ctx from reading runtime logs unless explicitly approved.
Audit shared directories for secrets before starting either agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, execute_shell, and broad network egress; ctx also has filesystem access and package-install/browser capabilities. If they operate on the same repo or mounted volume, concurrent writes and git mutations can corrupt state, and the profiles do not show locking or coordination.
conditions: IF ctx and OpenHands target the same filesystem path, write conflicts can occur.
IF both modify the same git branch without locks, history corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Serialize git operations through one agent at a time.
Freeze package installation during concurrent runs.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transaction coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx is designed to observe Claude Code events, so it can treat upstream outputs as authoritative context; OpenHands can act on shell/browser results and modify files. That creates a direct chain where one agent's output becomes the other's input and then downstream actions, with no verification step documented.
conditions: IF ctx forwards observed outputs into OpenHands prompts, errors can cascade.
IF OpenHands commits or executes actions based on ctx summaries, mistaken facts can become real changes.
mitigations: Insert a verification step between ctx summaries and OpenHands actions.
Require citations or source links for any factual claim before acting.
Limit OpenHands to dry-run mode for one iteration.
Review all commits before merge.
requires-engineering: add structured schemas and validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not state regulated-data handling, residency, or certification mismatches. The only concrete compliance-relevant clue is OpenHands handling model-provider API keys and ctx touching audit/runtime logs, which suggests logging/retention risk but not a documented breach path; the other agent is cited because the pairwise logging path is the concern.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into shared logs or runtime files, retention controls may diverge.
IF OpenHands is configured with a provider outside the required residency boundary, compliance risk increases.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared logs.
Review provider residency settings before launch.
Shorten log retention on both runtimes.
Separate secrets from general workspace files.
requires-engineering: document DPA/residency boundaries per runtime.
